chunks: And from him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"A woman may be returned [from the marriage] due to four conditions: leprosy, leprosy-like disease (al-judham), madness, and blindness (al-qaran), which is al-'afal. This is if the defect has not yet occurred upon her; but if it has occurred upon her, then there is no return."

And these two reports refer to the case where the defect occurs upon her after knowledge of her condition, so he is not entitled to return her, because that indicates consent. As for if the defect occurs upon her while he is unaware of her condition, then he learns, he has the right to return her in all cases, unless he chooses to keep her. And that which indicates this is what we have previously mentioned from the reports, containing the meaning that if he has consummated the marriage with her, she is entitled to the dowry because he made her private part permissible to him. So, if he did not have the right of return along with consummation, this statement would not have any meaning.
And that which adds clarification to this is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the four defects that allow a husband to return his wife in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the legal mechanism of *al-tadlis* (concealment of defects) in Shia jurisprudence, specifying that a husband may return his wife for leprosy, madness, or blindness if discovered post-consummation, provided he was unaware beforehand. The text clarifies that consummation does not forfeit this right, as the dowry is earned by the mere permission of the private part, a principle supported by the chain of transmission from Imam al-Sadiq. This ruling emphasizes the husband's option to retain or return the wife upon learning of the defect, balancing contractual fairness with marital stability.
